prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation by chemically induced proximity, from PROTACs to the molecular-glue mechanism of thalidomide-class drugs

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep targeted protein degradation as my preferred single-part configuration. The scientific core has not been challenged by anyone: a small molecule is designed to bring an E3 ubiquitin ligase and a target into proximity so that the cell destroys the protein instead of inhibiting it. That is a transferable design rule for recognition and assembly, and it has spread through chemical biology and medicinal chemistry far beyond its first examples. Maturity is better than the round-1 criticism suggests. The cereblon glue strand has years of approved clinical use with an established mechanism, and the PROTAC strand is two decades old, independently reproduced in hundreds of laboratories and in clinical trials. The critique I take most seriously is that PROTACs and glues are two lineages. I keep one citation because Handa's identification of cereblon is what turns the thalidomide-class drugs from an empirical accident into a designed mechanism, and it is the same principle of chemically induced proximity that Crews and Deshaies established with the engineered degrader. The citation is worded around the principle, not around a single drug class. Its acceptability is also the widest on the shortlist: six of the other seven members list it as an alternative, which I treat only as a hint about overlap and not as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The reservations remain real. No heterobifunctional PROTAC is approved, so the clinical proof for the most original half of the concept is pending. A three-name cap leaves out Ciulli, whose VHL ligand and ternary-complex structures made PROTACs drug-like, and Sakamoto, Kim and Gray, and several members (Aqvist, Chabes, Linke) would put Ciulli ahead of Handa. Base editing is further along on patient benefit in a narrow sense and has a cleaner attribution to a single design lineage, though I still read the 2020 CRISPR prize as a larger obstacle than its supporters do. Lipid nanoparticles have the largest demonstrated impact but the most difficult six-name attribution and an uncomfortable boundary with the 2023 Medicine prize.

responses.point: Aqvist backs Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli and calls Handa's cereblon work a mechanistic contribution and not a design invention, so a single citation spanning both strands risks being vague.
responses.response: This is the strongest objection to my configuration and I have thought about swapping Handa for Ciulli. I keep Handa because the quantitative standard you apply elsewhere points the same way: the cereblon mechanism is the only part of this field that is both clinically approved and mechanistically explained, and a PROTAC-only citation would rest on a drug class that is not yet approved. I accept that your Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli trio is the better answer if the committee wants a pure design-invention prize, and I would be comfortable with it. I would then ask that the citation be worded around induced proximity so that glues are not described as a footnote. I also agree with your own caution that phase separation remains the earlier-stage case and I would not support it ahead of degraders.

responses.point: Brzezinski keeps base editing first as the clearest attributable invention, with Liu, Komor and Gaudelli, and treats the 2020 CRISPR prize and the Kondo and Nishida Target-AID priority as the main risks.
responses.response: I agree base editing is a real chemical invention and I can vote for it if the committee consolidates there, which is why it stays my first alternative. My remaining disagreement is on increment. The 2020 citation honoured programmable targeting of Cas9 cleavage, and base editing builds a second layer on that platform, with prime editing likely to be pulled into the same story. Degradation opens a separate mechanistic area, the ubiquitin-proteasome system, so it adds more new chemistry per prize. I also take Chabes's point, which you endorse, that the adenine editor's evolved TadA has no independent parallel, and that does narrow the Kondo and Nishida problem. It does not remove it, and their exclusion is a real cost that a three-person cap cannot avoid.

responses.point: Chabes calls induced proximity a real design principle but doubts that a three-person prize can honour heterobifunctional PROTACs and cereblon glue degraders without distorting one, and ranks it a close second behind base editing.
responses.response: I take the distortion argument seriously and I do not think it can be fully dissolved. My answer is that the two strands share one mechanism, E3 ligase recruitment to a neo-substrate, and that Crews and Deshaies stated the general concept for engineered degraders while Handa identified how a drug discovered empirically acts through the same logic. A citation about chemically induced proximity covers both honestly. Your point about the absence of a PROTAC approval is fair and I conceded it in round 1. I disagree only on weight: approved cereblon-based drugs mean the principle is clinically proven, even if the heterobifunctional form is not yet.

responses.point: Sparr prefers ionizable lipid nanoparticles with Cullis, Hope and Madden and argues that the 2023 Medicine prize recognised nucleoside modification and not the delivery vehicle.
responses.response: I accept your argument that the 2023 overlap is weaker than I first feared, since the lipid particle was proven with siRNA in Onpattro before any mRNA vaccine. That moves B017 up in my thinking as an alternative. My difficulty is still the six-name group: Anderson, Langer and MacLachlan sit in a parallel lineage that a Vancouver trio excludes, and you yourself moved to Cullis, Hope and Madden in response to that. I cannot find a three-person cut that I would defend publicly without a priority dispute, which is the same difficulty I admit for degraders, but the degrader field's core principle is cleaner to state.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, proposes only Liu for base editing as an alternative and asks what a base-editing citation would credit that the CRISPR citation did not, while his own preference is nanopore sensing with a five-person attribution problem.
responses.response: On your question I think the defensible answer is that the 2020 prize honoured guided DNA cleavage while base editing is a defined chemical reaction, deamination, performed at one position without a double-strand break, so I would not call it a repeat. That is why I keep B006 as my first alternative. I agree with the attribution objections you and others raise against B048: I ranked it fifth, and I cannot see a three-name cut that leaves out a necessary contribution among Deamer, Branton, Kasianowicz, Bayley and Akeson. If the committee wants a nanopore prize the citation would need to state clearly that the ratchet and the engineered pore are the decisive steps.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the approved cereblon glue strand supports a prize citation despite there being no approved heterobifunctional PROTAC.
Whether Handa or Ciulli should hold the third place, since this decides whether the citation is about induced proximity as a whole or about engineered degraders alone.
Whether base editing consolidates enough support to command a majority, which would make it the more practical outcome than my preference.
How much weight to give the 2020 CRISPR prize against base editing, since I rate it higher as an obstacle than three members do.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict has emerged and I request no recusal. My postdoc mentors (Molly Stevens, Freddy Boey) and Linkoping colleagues are not credited on B068, B006 or B017. I repeat my disclosure of research overlap with Emma Sparr on self-assembly and peptide systems, and my translational and biosensor-company background, which may bias me toward chemistry-to-clinic cases such as degraders and lipid nanoparticles. Round 1 revealed nothing that changes this.
